course_profile.one_sentence_summary: Applied bachelor-level course on Data Science that combines mathematical modeling, Python implementation, and project labs across statistical learning, decision support, data intelligence, machine learning, neural networks, forecasting, credit scoring, and GIS analytics.
course_profile.short_summary: The course is positioned as an applied, Python-centered Data Science discipline aimed at helping students synthesize and verify mathematical models and develop specialized software for processing and analyzing heterogeneous data. Its structure combines a broad methodological core with progressively more practical labs and domain mini-projects in ERP/DSS, e-commerce forecasting, banking scoring, and GIS.

theoretical_understanding: Understand the Data Science processing chain from data acquisition through information extraction to knowledge use and visualization.
Explain core methodological areas of the course: statistical learning, decision support, data intelligence, machine learning, neural networks, credit scoring, and GIS.
Understand the mathematical logic behind least-squares regression, Kalman filtering, multicriteria scoring, clustering, and neural-network learning.
practical_implementation: Implement Python scripts for data parsing, preprocessing, analysis, visualization, and verification across multiple data modalities.
Build practical pipelines for regression, CP-SAT optimization, ML classification/clustering, ANN training, scoring, and geospatial analysis.
Use major Python data-science libraries in applied mini-project settings.
analysis_validation: Evaluate data quality, remove anomalies, and interpret model outputs for tabular, temporal, textual, and geospatial data.
Validate model behavior and verify developed scripts as a standard part of course practice.
Compare multiple algorithmic families for forecasting and applied decision-support tasks in an R&D style.
architecture_design: Translate applied domain problems into mathematical models and prototype software architectures.
Design prototype components for ERP/DSS, banking CRM scoring, and GIS systems.
research_and_prototyping: Carry out bounded R&D mini-projects rather than only scripted exercises.
Prototype advanced variants such as ANN architecture optimization, multifactor time-series analysis, and LLM-based text classification in higher-complexity tasks.

what_student_can_understand: How a broad Data Science workflow moves from raw data through mathematical modeling to actionable knowledge and decision support.
How core modeling families differ across regression, filtering, optimization, clustering, classification, neural networks, scoring, and GIS tasks.
what_student_can_build: Python prototypes for statistical-learning, ML, ANN, forecasting, scoring, and GIS scenarios.
Small applied systems or backend-style analytical components for ERP/DSS, bank CRM scoring, and geospatial workflows.
what_student_can_apply: Apply standard Python data-science libraries to parse, clean, model, visualize, and verify heterogeneous datasets.
Transfer course methods to practical problems in e-commerce, banking analytics, and GIS-oriented data processing.

evidence: The syllabus explicitly requires basic Python knowledge including syntax, data types, branching, functional and object-oriented programming, IDE work, and environment setup.
The syllabus states that successful course completion requires basic programming knowledge, algorithmization, and basic algorithms.
Prerequisite coursework listed in the syllabus includes algorithms and data structures across the supported degree programs.
The syllabus explicitly lists probability theory and mathematical statistics among the mathematical prerequisites.
The prerequisite block names matrix theory and degree-program courses in analytic geometry and linear algebra.
Discrete mathematics is explicitly included in the prerequisite knowledge and prerequisite coursework list.
The syllabus names OOP directly in the required Python background and in prerequisite coursework.
Module 2 repeatedly includes formalization of the task and preliminary data analysis as part of forecasting, scoring, and GIS practice.
Lab 1 requires file parsing and data parsing, and later labs repeat parsing as part of input data preparation.
The syllabus and multiple labs emphasize data research and preparation, cleaning, balancing, and normalization before modeling.
Visualization and analysis of results are repeated throughout the labs as an expected practical activity.

raw_mentions: training a regression model on Big Data with LSM
evidence: The syllabus and Lab 2 explicitly cover least-squares regression and polynomial regression for statistical learning.
Lecture 4 and Lab 2 explicitly include recurrent smoothing, alpha-beta, alpha-beta-gamma, and Kalman filtering.
Decision-support lectures and Lab 3 explicitly cover constraint programming and CP-SAT implementation with Google OR-Tools.
The syllabus names multicriteria decision analysis and scoring, while Lab 3 requires solving multicriteria optimization problems in code.
Lecture 8 and Lab 4 explicitly include OLAP as part of data intelligence practice.
Lecture 8 covers Text Mining / NLP, and Lab 4 includes mini projects in Text Mining plus an advanced text-classification R&D task.
The machine-learning block explicitly teaches clustering methods, and the scoring lab requires applicant clustering.
Lecture 10 and Lab 5 explicitly cover classification and identification, including decision trees, random forest, and image-related pattern recognition tasks.
Lecture 11/12 and Lab 6 explicitly cover perceptron construction, network architecture, training, and Python implementation with TensorFlow and Keras.

raw_mentions: forecasting dynamics of company performance indicators
evidence: The forecasting lab focuses on real numeric/time series and asks students to develop processing technologies for time-series forecasting using statistical learning, approximation, and deep learning.

raw_mentions: credit risks for banking CRM systems
evidence: Lecture 14 and Lab 8 explicitly frame a banking CRM credit-scoring task involving scoring, applicant clustering, and risk categorization.
The GIS topic and Lab 9 explicitly include searching, parsing, processing, and visualizing geodata from Shapefiles and vector maps using GeoPandas and GDAL.
Architecture design appears explicitly in the applied module for forecasting, scoring, and GIS, and several labs name architectural design of software systems as a target skill.
The syllabus defines verification as part of the course goal, and nearly all labs require verification of the developed implementations or obtained results.

lab_formats: Incremental Python laboratories with increasing functional complexity
Mini-project labs tied to course themes
Applied domain prototypes for ERP/DSS, e-commerce forecasting, bank scoring, and GIS
R&D-style advanced tasks for higher-complexity completion
expected_artifacts: Prototype components or mock systems for DSS, CRM scoring, forecasting, and GIS
implementation_tasks: Generate and analyze statistical samples and real datasets
Clean data, detect anomalies, fit regression models, and apply Kalman filtering
Implement CP-SAT and multicriteria decision-support models
Build OLAP, text-mining, and related data-intelligence mini-projects
Implement clustering, classification, and computer-vision style ML pipelines
Construct, train, and apply perceptrons and neural networks
Develop time-series forecasting modules for commercial indicators
Develop a bank scoring backend prototype with scoring and applicant clustering
Process and visualize Shapefile-based geospatial data
engineering_practices: Comparative R&D exploration of alternative methods

intra_course_relations.reason: The applied module repeatedly orders work as task formalization followed by architecture design and software development.
Labs start by obtaining/parsing data and then cleaning, balancing, or normalizing them before modeling.
The statistical-learning block explicitly cleans anomalous observations and optimizes data models before regression training.
The scoring lab explicitly includes cleaning, balancing, and normalization before clustering and related ML tasks.
Scoring is presented as a multicriteria evaluation approach, and the scoring lecture includes a mathematical scoring model.
The banking scoring task requires clustering applicants alongside building a scoring assessment.
Both are taught together in the DSS/ERP block as optimization-oriented approaches for automated decision support.
The ANN lab frames neural networks as practical technologies for classification, identification, and forecasting after the classical ML block.
The ANN lab and forecasting lab both explicitly use neural-network methods for time-series prediction.
The GIS lab directly couples geodata processing with digital map visualization and analysis of results.
Applied labs repeatedly progress from architecture/design and implementation toward verification of the developed scripts and systems.
